biography.label: Biography / life writing
biography.date_label: Ancient roots · Strachey 1918 · Davis 1995 · crosses fields
biography.description: Uses individual and collective lives to ask historical questions about character, social relations, power and experience. Documentary reconstruction, psychoanalytic interpretation, contextual comparison and relational trajectories pose different problems. Authors, subjects, editors and collaborators shape the surviving account.

representative_people.works: Translation and editorial assistance acknowledged in Women on the Margins (1995)

biography.scope_note: A genre and set of methods with ancient and varied roots, not inherently great-man history, psychohistory or microstoria. The selected roster combines earlier practices, modern historical work and critics. Davis’s comparison preserves religious and colonial differences; her imagined prologue is not historical testimony. Bourdieu questions narrated coherence without banning life histories; Levi emphasizes choices within constraints and investigates group formation. Biography can explain wider relations, but its scale and source gaps remain subjects of criticism. Non-European traditions and original translation witnesses require further research; the current selection is not exhaustive.

strands.title: Labour lives and collective authorship
strands.focus: Torr’s Mann project draws on biographical materials and collaborative preparation. The incomplete continuation, manuscript/publication distinction and Murphy’s criticism make the production of a life history visible.
strands.works: Tom Mann and His Times, vol. 1 (1956); further fragments edited by E. P. Thompson, Our History 26–27 (1962)

strands.title: Individual reconstruction and social explanation
strands.focus: Power pairs lives with estate books, letters, household advice and material remains. Her personal treatment is a teaching method; Postan’s later reconstruction makes editorial mediation visible.

strands.title: Biographical sympathy and revision through evidence
strands.focus: Wedgwood’s two Strafford treatments offer a case of reassessment through new sources and scholarship. Woolrych’s criticism of eulogy remains visible alongside his appreciation.
strands.works: Strafford (1935); Thomas Wentworth ... A Revaluation (1961); Woolrych memoir (1998)

strands.title: A life as narrative vehicle: reach and missing evidence
strands.focus: Tuchman selects Coucy to travel across a turbulent period but acknowledges documentary limits. Stone questions whether that organizing device yields a sufficiently understood person or explains wider institutions.
strands.works: A Distant Mirror (1978), foreword; Stone review (1978)

strands.title: Whose lives and which particulars?
strands.focus: Johnson’s private lives, Brown’s collective recovery and Woolf’s changed criteria show different arguments about biographical significance. They are not a single progression from great men to ordinary people.
strands.works: Rambler 60 (1750); The Black Man (1863); The Art of Biography (1939)

strands.title: Narrated unity and relational trajectories
strands.focus: Bourdieu asks how institutions, interviews and retrospective storytelling produce coherent selves, and proposes trajectories within changing fields. Life history remains possible under relational scrutiny.

strands.title: Scale, norms and bounded agency
strands.focus: Levi distinguishes several uses of lives and locates choices within conflicting norms. Group coherence becomes a question to investigate, not an automatic starting assumption.

strands.title: Contextual reconstruction and its limits
strands.focus: Roche’s Ménétra and Venturi’s Diderot illustrate different contextual procedures in Levi’s account. Context can illuminate gaps while itself requiring a dynamic explanation.
strands.works: Journal de ma vie (1982); Jeunesse de Diderot (1939), mediated by Levi (1989)

strands.title: Comparative lives, religion and colonial power
strands.focus: Davis holds similarities and differences together, tests her categories through an imagined prologue and rejects a single progressive sequence. Marginality does not prevent participation in colonial domination.
strands.works: Women on the Margins (1995), selected primary passages

strands.title: Publishing, translating and cutting a life record
strands.focus: Davis compares Glikl editions with different treatment of stories and moral commentary. Pappenheim’s role as translator is distinguished from the clinical narrative about her.

strands.title: Teaching, source discovery and collaborative work
strands.focus: Davis names course development, source suggestions, translation, archives, libraries and editing as resources. A selective roster does not exhaust the acknowledged labor behind the book.

strands.title: Psychoanalytic interpretation and critical limits
strands.focus: Erikson’s 1970 retrospective supplies a primary account of his Luther interpretation, while the original 1958 book remains unread. Levi’s generic psychobiography judgment is not an Erikson-specific rebuttal.
strands.works: Young Man Luther (1958); Levi (1989), methodological discussion; Erikson, Autobiographic Notes (1970), p. 750

strands.title: Individual life and historical surroundings
strands.focus: Dilthey’s biographical work and later reflections join individual initiative to institutions and cultural systems. Biography brings contextual factors into view that recollection alone may not supply.
strands.works: Leben Schleiermachers I (1870), through scholarly discussion

strands.title: Psychological motives and limits of inference
strands.focus: Namier argues that professed reasons may conceal unconscious processes, but insists that psychological origins alone do not refute an argument. His warning about fragmentary evidence limits the use of psychological explanations in historical lives.

annales.label: Annales
annales.description: A changing journal-centered constellation: comparative inquiry, geography, economic series, belief, social imaginaries, and later experiments with representation and scale. Cultural questions belong to the founders as well as subsequent projects.

strands.title: Founding exchange and historical problems
strands.focus: The 1929 editors invite exchanges across specialties, without claiming to invent economic/social history. Belief and culture are present from the outset.
strands.works: “À nos lecteurs” (1929); The Royal Touch; The Problem of Unbelief

strands.title: Braudel’s multiple historical times
strands.focus: Models must survive comparison with changing evidence; their failure matters. Braudel’s productive Lévi-Strauss borrowing and Chartier’s later objection to an explanatory hierarchy mark disagreements within this conversation.

strands.title: Economic series and agrarian cycles
strands.focus: Labrousse’s price/income inquiry and Le Roy Ladurie’s population/resource model differ in objects and scale; quantification does not define every Annales project.

strands.title: Belief, imagined order and representations
strands.focus: Le Goff’s purgatory, Duby’s social hierarchy and Chartier’s representations offer different historical constructions, not one timeless collective mentality.
strands.works: La Naissance du Purgatoire (1981); Les Trois Ordres (1978); “Le monde comme représentation” (1989)

strands.title: Traces, questions and comparative reasoning
strands.focus: Bloch distinguishes deliberate from unintended testimony and origins from causes. Present observation can inform questions, without making past and present identical.

strands.title: Historical psychology and its criticisms
strands.focus: Febvre historicizes collective feelings with psychological resources and a critical Huizinga reading. Walker later questions universal claims about what people could think.
strands.works: “La sensibilité et l’histoire” (1941); The Problem of Unbelief (1942); Walker review (1983)

strands.title: Village reconstruction and mediated voices
strands.focus: Montaillou uses inquisitorial records for intimate social history. Such records do not provide unfiltered speech, and small scale alone does not establish Italian microstoria affiliation.

strands.title: Models and the critical turn
strands.focus: Lepetit and the editors ask how explicit models and categories can be assessed through historical evidence. Their reconsideration retains comparison and collective inquiry.
strands.works: “L’histoire et les modèles” (1988); Les Formes de l’expérience (1995)

strands.title: Observation, exceptions and generalization
strands.focus: The 1988 editorial explicitly engages microhistory; Revel’s later collective volume explores varying scale. This is an exchange, not a declaration that micro-level explanation replaces all larger patterns.

strands.title: Books as material and social productions
strands.focus: Febvre’s plan/revision and Martin’s drafting form a specific collaboration. Printing is situated among economic, technical and cultural conditions.

strands.title: Women’s history and collaborative limits
strands.focus: Duby and Perrot co-direct a multi-author project. Its Western scope and Annales’ earlier limited openings matter; feminist history has other origins and commitments.

memory.scope_note: Halbwachs’s social frameworks, Nora’s commemorative sites, and Samuel’s popular uses of the past are distinct projects. Communicative and cultural memory are the Assmann project’s distinctions, not a universal taxonomy. War mourning, Holocaust memorials and feminist subjectivity require different historical explanations; this selection remains weighted toward European debates. Jelin’s Argentina project adds a pre-2000 case beyond Europe; it does not represent all Latin American memory work.

cdn_working_class.label: Canadian working-class history
cdn_working_class.date_label: Earlier institutional histories (Logan 1948) · Labour/Le Travailleur founded 1976 · Palmer 1979, Kealey 1980 · debate over culture 1981 · gender and family 1989–93 · selected later works
cdn_working_class.description: Canadian working-class history took shape in the 1970s as a new labour history of class, culture and community, set against an older institutional history of unions, labour politics and industrial relations (Logan 1948; Abella 1973; Bercuson 1974). The Canadian Committee on Labour History founded Labour/Le Travailleur in 1976. Palmer’s skilled workers in Hamilton (1979), Kealey’s Toronto workers (1980) and their history of the Knights of Labor (1982) were among its early monographs. In 1981 Kenneth McNaught framed the contrast as ‘E. P. Thompson vs Harold Logan’ and, by a later account, objected that social historians took a revolutionary goal as history’s purpose; Bercuson questioned working-class culture as an explanatory framework, and Kealey defended class analysis and culture. Social historians of poverty and the state widened the field: Copp’s Montreal working class (1974), Finkel on business and reform (1979), Struthers on unemployment (1983). Feminist historians remade it from within: Sangster on women on the left (1989), Parr’s gender of breadwinners (1990) and Bradbury’s working families (1993). Rouillard wrote the history of Quebec unionism in French (1989), and Heron’s Workers’ Revolt in Canada (1998) took the 1917–25 upheaval as a national subject. Palmer’s Descent into Discourse (1990) attacked the linguistic turn in social history. In 2000 Morton argued that the journal’s founding team had concealed a decade of stasis. Later work turned to deindustrialization (High 2003), the history of the left (McKay 2008) and Indigenous labour and the settler order.
cdn_working_class.representative_figures_and_works: Logan, Trade Unions in Canada (1948); Abella, Nationalism, Communism, and Canadian Labour (1973); Bercuson, Confrontation at Winnipeg (1974); Copp, The Anatomy of Poverty (1974); Labour/Le Travailleur (1976); Palmer, A Culture in Conflict (1979); Finkel, Business and Social Reform in the Thirties (1979); Kealey, Toronto Workers Respond to Industrial Capitalism (1980); McNaught, Bercuson and Kealey (1981); Kealey and Palmer, Dreaming of What Might Be (1982); Struthers, No Fault of Their Own (1983); Palmer, Working-Class Experience (1983; 1992); Heron, Working in Steel (1988); Rouillard, Histoire du syndicalisme au Québec (1989); Sangster, Dreams of Equality (1989); Palmer, Descent into Discourse (1990); Parr, The Gender of Breadwinners (1990); Lutz, “After the Fur Trade” (1992); Bradbury, Working Families (1993); Kealey, Workers and Canadian History (1995); Heron, The Workers’ Revolt in Canada (1998); Morton and Sangster in Labour/Le Travail 46 (2000). Later: High, Industrial Sunset (2003); McKay, Reasoning Otherwise (2008); Burrill (2019); Finkel on Palmer (2021).
cdn_working_class.scope_note: A national research field within labour history. The ‘old’ institutional history and the ‘new’ labour history are positions in a debate, not successive stages; Bercuson and McNaught are critics (their 1981 essays are now checked through Bercuson’s abstract and Finkel’s account of McNaught), and Morton’s 2000 critique comes from outside the new labour history. Marxist and Thompsonian resources are documented by McNaught’s title and Kealey’s defence of class analysis; no single theory is attributed to the field. Gender historians (Sangster, Parr, Bradbury) are treated mainly in Canadian women’s and gender history; they appear here for their working-class histories. Quebec labour history in French (Rouillard) is part of the field and of Quebec historiography. Poverty and welfare-state histories overlap with political history. Immigrant workers (Avery) are in the immigration entry; Indigenous labour is a strand, not a claim of adoption. Palmer’s Descent into Discourse (1990) is placed here as a critique of the linguistic turn, not as a critique of women’s history. McKay’s left history is a post-2000 contributor row; his main entry is Liberal order framework.

strands.title: Unions, labour politics and industrial relations
strands.focus: Logan’s history of unions (1948), Abella on the CIO, communism and nationalism (1973), and Bercuson on the Winnipeg General Strike (1974): the institutional history against which the new labour history defined itself.

strands.title: The new labour history: class, culture and community
strands.focus: Palmer’s skilled workers in Hamilton (1979), Kealey’s Toronto workers (1980), their Knights of Labor (1982) and Palmer’s synthesis (1983; 1992). Kealey also engages the US new labour history of Gutman and Montgomery (1990, title-level).

strands.title: Labour/Le Travail and the CCLH
strands.focus: The Canadian Committee on Labour History founded Labour/Le Travailleur in 1976: the journal’s archive and Crossref date volume 1 to 1976, with Palmer, Kealey and Rouillard (in French) among its contributors. Freeman names Kealey, Palmer and Sangster among the founding generation. The journal is also the site of the 1981 and 2000 exchanges.

strands.title: The 1981 debate over culture and class
strands.focus: McNaught frames the decade as ‘E. P. Thompson vs Harold Logan’ (CHR 1981) and, by Finkel’s account, objects that social historians took a revolutionary goal as the purpose of historical writing. In Labour/Le Travailleur 7, Bercuson questions working-class culture as an explanatory framework and the priority of history “from the bottom up”; Kealey strongly defends class analysis and culture. Kealey’s essay was a companion to Bercuson’s, not a reply: both were first given at the McGill ‘Class and Culture’ conference in March 1980. His collected essays (1995) reprint it. McNaught’s essay is read only through Finkel.

strands.title: Poverty, unemployment and the welfare state
strands.focus: Copp’s Montreal working class (1974), Finkel on business and social reform (1979) and Struthers on unemployment and the welfare state (1983).

strands.title: Gender, family and class
strands.focus: Women on the left (Sangster 1989), the gender of breadwinners (Parr 1990) and working families (Bradbury 1993). Sangster (2000) describes feminist challenges to the initially ‘masculinist’ shape of working-class history and calls to integrate race and ethnicity.

strands.title: Quebec labour history
strands.focus: Rouillard’s history of Quebec unionism (1989) in French; Copp and Bradbury on Montreal’s working class. Shared with Quebec historiography.

strands.title: Steel, revolt and national scope
strands.focus: Heron’s steelworkers (1988) and The Workers’ Revolt in Canada, 1917–1925 (1998), a national frame for the post-war upheaval (title-level).

strands.title: Discourse, stasis and critique, 1990–2000
strands.focus: Palmer’s Descent into Discourse (1990) attacks the reification of language in social history, a critique of the linguistic turn (Finkel). Morton (2000) argues the L/LT team’s domination concealed stasis and decline; Sangster (2000) records the feminist critique and the unsettling effect of post-structuralism and the left’s decline.

strands.title: Indigenous labour and the settler order
strands.focus: Lutz (1992) treats Aboriginal people in British Columbia as a labouring class. Burrill (2019, after 2000) proposes a settler-order framework that puts settler workers’ ongoing theft of Indigenous land into Canadian working-class history.

strands.title: Deindustrialization

strands.title: Histories of the Canadian left (after 2000)
strands.focus: McKay’s Reasoning Otherwise (2008), first of a planned three-volume history of the left from 1890 to the Winnipeg General Strike; read by many PhDs who engage working-class history.

cdn_women_gender.label: Canadian women's & gender history
cdn_women_gender.date_label: Earlier women writers of history (recovered by Boutilier and Prentice 1997) and Cleverdon’s suffrage history 1950 · collections and studies 1976–79 · Collectif Clio 1982 · Prentice et al. 1988 · Parr 1990 · Left History exchange 1995–96 · selected publication milestones, not boundaries
cdn_women_gender.description: Canadian women's history studies women as historical actors in Canada and, increasingly from the 1990s, gender as a relation shaping work, family, politics, law and the state. Earlier women wrote national, local and regional history, recovered by Boutilier and Prentice (1997); Cleverdon studied the suffrage movement (1950); collections and studies of reform and women's organizations followed in the later 1970s (Cook and Mitchinson; Strong-Boag; Kealey). Two syntheses had different starting points. The Collectif Clio's L'histoire des femmes au Québec depuis quatre siècles (1982) rejected a male-centred history presented as everyone's history; Prentice and colleagues' Canadian Women: A History (1988) offered a collaborative survey. Studies of women and war (Pierson), women on the left (Sangster), working families in Montreal (Bradbury) and housewives in the Depression (Baillargeon) joined the field to labour and family history. Parr's comparison of two Ontario towns (1990) challenged assumptions about the separateness of gender and class roles. In the 1990s historians argued over whether gender history extended or displaced women's history: Pierson weighed the turn to deconstruction and Scott's theory of gender against experience and voice (1991), and Sangster's 'Beyond Dichotomies' (1995), by her later account, protested a hierarchy that set gender history above a 'limited' women's history; replies in Left History defended gender history (1996). Later work examined masculinity and gendered political languages (Morgan), sexuality and the law, and postwar domesticity and consumption (Parr, Korinek, Fahrni). Lévesque asked how far Quebec historiography had integrated women (1997); Quebec women's history is treated mainly under Quebec historiography.
cdn_women_gender.representative_figures_and_works: Earlier women writers of history: Machar, Skinner, Skelton, Esther Clark Wright, Neatby, Ormsby, Daveluy, as recovered in Boutilier and Prentice, eds., Creating Historical Memory (1997); Cleverdon, The Woman Suffrage Movement in Canada (1950). Cook and Mitchinson, eds., The Proper Sphere (1976); Strong-Boag, The Parliament of Women (1976); Kealey, ed., A Not Unreasonable Claim (1979). Collectif Clio, L'histoire des femmes au Québec depuis quatre siècles (1982; Quebec Women, 1987); Prentice et al., Canadian Women: A History (1988). Pierson, "They're Still Women After All" (1986); Danylewycz, Taking the Veil (1987); Strong-Boag, The New Day Recalled (1988); Sangster, Dreams of Equality (1989); Lévesque, La norme et les déviantes (1989); Parr, The Gender of Breadwinners (1990); Baillargeon, Ménagères au temps de la crise (1991); Mitchinson, The Nature of Their Bodies (1991); Bradbury, Working Families (1993); Dubinsky, Improper Advances (1993). Debate: Pierson (1991); Parr (1995); Sangster (1995, 1996); Iacovetta and Kealey (1996); Dubinsky and Marks (1996); Lévesque (1997); Sangster's retrospect (2011). Morgan, Public Men and Virtuous Women (1996); McPherson, Morgan and Forestell, eds., Gendered Pasts (1999); Parr, Domestic Goods (1999); Korinek, Roughing It in the Suburbs (2000); Christie, Engendering the State (2000). Comparison: Van Kirk, "Many Tender Ties" (1980); Perry, On the Edge of Empire (2001). Later readings: Fahrni (2005), Campbell (2009), Bienvenue on Daveluy (2018), Bienvenue and Dorais, eds., Profession historienne? (2023). Ramsay Cook and Wendy Mitchinson, eds., The Proper Sphere (1976).
cdn_women_gender.scope_note: A Canadian research field joining women's history and gender history; the entry does not decide the 1990s argument between them. Quebec women's history (Collectif Clio, Lévesque, Baillargeon) has its primary treatment in Quebec historiography; this entry keeps those authors' work on family, work and sexuality and a critique edge to Quebec historiography. Fur-trade women (Van Kirk) and gender and empire (Perry) are treated mainly in Indigenous–newcomer relations & fur-trade history and Settler colonialism and appear here as comparison rows; sexuality, law and regulation overlap with Moral regulation; childhood and family with Childhood, youth & family in Canada. Palmer's Descent into Discourse is treated in Canadian working-class history, as a critique of the linguistic turn, not of women's history.

strands.title: Earlier women writers of history
strands.focus: Women wrote Canadian history long before women’s history was a field: popular, local and regional historians (Machar, Skinner, Esther Clark Wright), the independent scholar Isabel Skelton, and a few university historians, among them Hilda Neatby and Margaret Ormsby, the CHA’s first and second women presidents (1962–63; 1965–66). In French Canada, Marie-Claire Daveluy wrote on New France. Most wrote national, local, fur-trade or political history; only Skelton (who “sought to write women back into Canadian history”, per Coulter’s reading of Crowley) and Daveluy (Bienvenue 2018) are documented as writing women in. They are earlier women writers of history, not founders of women’s history. Boutilier and Prentice’s Creating Historical Memory (1997) recovered this work and asked how professionalization masculinized history; the editors note that their subjects come mainly from “the white, Anglo-Celtic segment of society”. Cleverdon’s suffrage history (1950) is the earlier study of women that PhDs still cite. Bienvenue and Dorais (2023) extend the recovery to French Canada (after 2000).
strands.works: Boutilier and Prentice, eds., Creating Historical Memory (1997); Prentice, “Laying Siege to the History Professoriate” (1997); Cleverdon (1950); Bienvenue on Daveluy (2018)

cdn_military.label: Canadian military history
cdn_military.date_label: Duguid’s only official volume 1938 · Stacey’s official histories 1955–70 · Nicholson’s replacement CEF history 1962 · Broken Promises 1977 · war-and-society studies 1986–93 · Walker on race and recruitment 1989 · Valour and the Horror broadcast and hearings 1992 · Vance 1997 · selected later works
cdn_military.description: Canadian military history has three overlapping modes: official and operational history, war and society, and memory and public history. Early work was largely official history, published by authority of the Minister of National Defence. Duguid’s official history of the Great War produced only one volume (1938); Nicholson’s Canadian Expeditionary Force (1962) replaced it. Stacey wrote volumes I (1955) and III (1960) of the Official History of the Canadian Army in the Second World War, and his Arms, Men and Governments (1970) made war policy a subject; Stanley’s Canada’s Soldiers (1954) called Canadians ‘an unmilitary people’. Conscription and French-Canadian participation recur, from Armstrong’s Crisis of Quebec (1937) to Granatstein and Hitsman’s Broken Promises (1977) and francophone histories of the 22nd Battalion (Gagnon 1986) and of bilingualism in the forces (Pariseau and Bernier 1987). From the 1980s war-and-society history turned to soldiers, veterans, psychiatry and women: Morton’s military and political histories (1981, 1985), veterans’ return (Morton and Wright 1987), battle exhaustion (Copp and McAndrew 1990) and Pierson on wartime womanhood (1986). Walker (1989) studied the enlistment of visible minorities, and Dempsey Prairie First Nations soldiers (1999). Popular history (Berton’s Vimy, 1986) and the CBC series The Valour and the Horror (1992), which led to Senate hearings and an ombudsman’s report, made military history a major public controversy. Vance’s Death So Noble (1997) treated the Great War as a cultural force in interwar memory. Cook (2002, 2006) showed that the records and narratives of Stacey’s officers were neither neutral nor unbiased.

cdn_military.scope_note: A research field with three overlapping modes: official and operational history, war and society, and memory and public history. They are not successive stages; official historians also wrote policy history, and war-and-society historians also wrote operations. Popular history (Berton) and public controversy are included as part of the field’s public life, not as academic scholarship. Francophone work on conscription and French-Canadian participation is part of the field and meets Quebec historiography. Several roster people are treated mainly elsewhere (Stanley, Granatstein, Copp, Bercuson, Pierson, Vance); they appear for specific works. Imperial, naval and air histories and the Royal Military College tradition are thin in this selection. Critics of militarized memory (McKay and Swift) are after 2000. Black and Japanese-Canadian soldiers appear through Walker (1989, scholarly) and two community and veteran histories (Ruck 1987, Ito 1984). The Valour and the Horror controversy is a strand here, called a major public-history controversy on a contemporary witness (Dick 1993); Carr’s later treatment (CHR 2005) is unread, so it is not called a defining historiographical controversy.

who_killed_debate.label: The 'Who Killed Canadian History?' debate
who_killed_debate.date_label: Roots: Cook 1967, Careless 1969 · Bliss's 'Privatizing the Mind' and the JCS replies 1991–92 · Strong-Boag's CHA address 1994 · Granatstein's book 1998 · CHR replies (McKillop, Palmer) and francophone reviews 1998–99 · CHR forum, Buckner, McKay and Osborne 2000 · Dummitt and Dawson 2009
who_killed_debate.description: A quarrel among English-Canadian historians in the 1990s over whether national history had been lost, taught here as a moment in the profession's view of itself, not as current practice: few recent theses cite its texts. It had two phases. In 1991–92 Bliss's 'Privatizing the Mind' argued that intense specialization had replaced older historians' concern with explaining the country, and asked historians to remember that their subject was Canada. A 'Point-Counterpoint' in the same journal answered him: Gregory Kealey's class history was 'neither privatizing, nor sundering' (1992), and Linda Kealey, Pierson, Sangster and Strong-Boag asked whose 'national' history was being lamented. Strong-Boag's 1994 presidential address answered 'neo-conservative laments' by indicting an old history of white male elites. In 1998 Granatstein's Who Killed Canadian History? took the charge to a public audience. In the Canadian Historical Review McKillop (1999) argued that Granatstein's narrow national history was itself political legitimation, and Palmer offered a dissident view. Francophone reviewers answered too: Dubuc read a lament for political history; Dumont, an indictment of social historians built on wrong facts about Quebec schooling. It grew from the 'limited identities' of region, culture and class that Cook named (1967) and Careless popularized (1969). In 2000 Létourneau proposed a narrative of Canada beyond unitarist and fragmenting versions, Cook called identities contingent and multiple, Buckner revisited limited identities, and McKay offered the liberal order framework as a way past the impasse. Dummitt and Dawson (2009) sought to move beyond political-versus-social history.
who_killed_debate.representative_figures_and_works: Roots: Cook, "Canadian Centennial Cerebrations" (1967); Careless, "'Limited Identities' in Canada" (1969); Reid (1987); Buckner (1988). Phase one: Bliss, "Privatizing the Mind" (1991–92), answered in the JCS Point-Counterpoint by G. Kealey (1992) and L. Kealey, Pierson, Sangster and Strong-Boag (1992); Strong-Boag, "Contested Space" (1994). Phase two: Granatstein, Who Killed Canadian History? (1998), answered in the CHR by McKillop, "A View from the Trenches" (1999) and Palmer, "Of Silences and Trenches" (1999); Strong-Boag's review (1999); francophone reviews by Dionne (RHAF 1998), Bouvier, Fahmy-Eid, Jedwab and Slogar, and Dubuc (BHP 1999) and Dumont (CHA Bulletin 1999). Reassessments: Létourneau and the CHR forum (2000); Cook, "Identities Are Not Like Hats" (2000); Buckner, "'Limited Identities' Revisited" (2000); McKay, "The Liberal Order Framework" (2000); Osborne (2000). Later: Dummitt and Dawson, eds., Contesting Clio's Craft (2009); Hamilton (2012).
who_killed_debate.scope_note: A debate entry measured through its texts, not its people, and written as a teaching entry about the profession's self-understanding rather than current practice: any core debate text is cited by 34 of 1,303 strict 2009–2026 History PhDs (2.6%), falling to 2.0% in 2020–26. It has two phases: Bliss and the Journal of Canadian Studies replies (1991–92), and Granatstein and the Canadian Historical Review replies (1998–99); the 1992 JCS pieces answer Bliss, not Who Killed Canadian History?. Most participants' citations in the PhD corpus come from their other work. Bliss and Granatstein's scholarship is in Political, international & national history; Bliss's main entry is Political, international & national history; this entry keeps his debate row (user decision 2026-10-12). The replying fields are Canadian working-class history, Canadian women's & gender history and Canadian regional history. Several replies are characterized by title only (Gregory Kealey 1992; Kealey, Pierson, Sangster and Strong-Boag 1992; Palmer 1999). The exchange among the main protagonists was English-Canadian, but francophone historians answered Granatstein in RHAF, the Bulletin d'histoire politique and the CHA Bulletin (1998–99); no francophone reply to Bliss was found. Létourneau's 2000 CHR essay is the francophone voice in the 2000 reassessments. Quebec's own debate over national and political history (the BHP from 1992, Bélanger 1997, later the 2006–07 school programme) ran separately; its checked texts do not cite Bliss or Granatstein, and it is related here only by comparison. Osborne's school-history essay links to history education, which the atlas does not treat as an entry.
